blocks.note: The one file that knows how to get a real price. There is no official Google Flights interface, so this code builds the request a browser would send and reads the page that comes back. That makes it the most fragile file in the project, and the header is honest about it: when Google changes the page, lerPagina raises a clear error instead of pretending there are no flights. It also runs on its own: node voos.ts GRU LIS 2026-12-12.

The shape of a flight, and the contract the rest of the project is written against. The spreadsheet, the checker, the tools and the watcher all read these ten fields and nothing else. duracao_min is minutes, preco is the total for every passenger in reais, saida is "HH:MM" and chegada carries the day too, because a long flight lands on another date.

Your own invented metric, in two numbers: an hour of travel is worth 30 reais and a stop is worth 200. Nothing about this comes from Google. Because it is yours, the writer is explicitly allowed to quote the rule, which is hard-coded as an exception in harness/agente.ts (around line 235) and explained in rule 5 of the writer's instructions in harness/agentes.ts.

Turns a flight into one comparable number: the price plus the cost of the time plus the cost of the stops. A non-stop flight that is 300 reais dearer can win. Used by planilha.ts for the summary tab, by descreverVoo in harness/ferramentas.ts, and by the custo_beneficio sort order in filtrar_voos.

Google takes the whole search as one base64 string holding a Protobuf message, in the "tfs" parameter. The next six functions build that by hand, byte by byte. CLASSES maps your class names to the numbers Google uses, 1 through 4.

varint: how Protobuf writes an integer. Seven bits per byte, with the top bit meaning "another byte follows". The loop pushes (numero & 127) | 128, which keeps the low seven bits and sets the continue flag, then shifts right by seven. The >>>= is the unsigned shift, which matters because the signed one would mangle large values. The last byte goes out without the flag.

A plain number field. Protobuf identifies a field by its number shifted left three places, with the low three bits saying what type follows. Shifting left by 3 with no type bits set means "a varint comes next".

A length-delimited field, so the tag gets type bits 2: the field number, then the length, then the bytes. This is the one that lets a field hold another field, which is how the origin nests inside the leg below.
A string as raw bytes. Buffer.from gives UTF-8 bytes and the spread turns the Buffer into a plain array, so it can be concatenated with the other byte arrays.

One leg of the trip. Field 2 is the date as text. Field 13 is the origin, and notice it is campoBytes wrapping another campoBytes: Google expects the airport inside its own field 2, one level deeper. Field 14 is the destination the same way. Getting this nesting wrong is the classic way to receive an empty page.
Passengers are a list of numbers rather than counts: a 1 for each adult and a 2 for each child. Two adults and a child is [1, 1, 2]. Array(n).fill(v) builds each run.

The finished request: field 3 is the leg, field 8 the passenger list, field 9 the class number, and field 19 set to 2 means one way only. Then the whole byte array becomes base64. Everything in this project is one-way searches, and a round trip is handled as two separate searches added together, which is why combinar_ida_e_volta ends its answer with a warning that buying them as one ticket may cost something else. Exported so teste.ts can check the output byte for byte, without the network.

Google sends dates as [2026, 12, 12] and times as [15, 5], and a zero can simply be missing, so [8] means 08:00 and [null, 31] means 00:31. Date.UTC handles the month minus one, because JavaScript months start at zero, and the ?? 0 fallbacks fill the holes. Dividing by 60000 turns milliseconds into minutes, which is the unit the duration maths below works in.
Two small formatters: zero-pad a number to two digits, and print one of Google's time arrays as "HH:MM", with the same missing-value fallbacks.

The parser. The flights are not in the HTML you can see: they sit in a <script class="ds:1"> tag as a JSON blob. Line 92 finds that marker and line 93 is the honest failure: no marker means the page changed, and the error says so instead of reporting zero flights. Reporting zero would be worse than crashing, because you would believe the route is empty.

Cutting the JSON out by hand. Line 94 takes everything between the end of the opening tag and the closing one. Line 95 takes what follows "data:" up to the last comma. Line 96 is Google's own way of saying "I found nothing": when the blob ends in errorHasStatus: true, that is a real empty result, so return an empty list rather than an error.

Everything from here is inside a try, so any surprise in the shape of the data becomes one clear message at the bottom instead of a random crash. Line 101 covers the other empty shape: a route that does not exist comes back as an empty array.

pagina[3][0] is the list of flights. Those bare numbers are the price of reading an undocumented page, and they are the first thing that breaks when Google changes anything. Line 104 digs out the price, and line 105 skips a flight that has none, which really happens: better to drop it than to guess a number.
item[0][2] is the list of segments: one for a direct flight, three for a trip with two stops. The first segment holds the real departure and the last one the real arrival.

The duration, and the comment explains why the obvious way fails: you cannot subtract departure from arrival, because the two airports are in different time zones. Instead each segment's own flying time (index 11) is added, and for every segment after the first the layover is added too, as this segment's departure minus the previous segment's arrival, both converted to absolute minutes by paraMinutos. That is the only correct way to do it with the data Google gives.

Building the flight record. The airlines are joined with " + ", so a LATAM and Iberia itinerary reads as one name. Stops are segments minus one. The arrival string includes the day and month from the last segment's arrival date, which is why a 22:10 departure can read "13/12 12:30". The link is the human search URL built further down, the same for every flight in the search.

The catch turns any parsing surprise into "the page data came in a new format" plus the original message, which points you at the page rather than at your own logic. Line 135 sorts cheapest first, and every other file in the project assumes that order: the tools call the first element the cheapest without re-sorting.

The guard between the model and Google. The comment states the reason plainly: the AI picks these values, so the code checks them before they leave the machine. It is exported and reused by the exam's fake search in harness/avaliar.ts, so the fake refuses exactly what the real one refuses.
Both ends must be exactly three capital letters. A city name, a typo or a shell flag like --help is rejected here and never reaches the network.

The date check in two halves. The regex pins the format, and then the date has to survive a round trip through Date and come back identical. That second half is what rejects 2026-02-30: JavaScript happily turns it into 2 March, and the round trip catches the silent change.

At least one adult, no negative children, and nine passengers maximum, which is Google's own limit. Number.isInteger also rejects 1.5 and NaN, which is what you get when a model sends something strange and coercion does not save you.
The class has to be one of the four keys of CLASSES, since line 69 would otherwise put undefined into the request and the search would come back wrong rather than failing.

The real search. Line 158 validates first. Line 160 builds the parameters: the tfs blob, hl=pt-BR for Portuguese labels and curr=BRL so prices come in reais. Line 161 builds the clickable human link that goes into every flight record, which is what you press to buy.

The request, with three hard-won details. The comment names the first: without &tfu=EgQIABABIgA, Google returns only its "best flights" and leaves the cheapest ones out, which quietly ruins the whole bot. The User-Agent is a normal browser string, because the plain Node one gets a different page. And AbortSignal.timeout(30000) gives up after thirty seconds instead of hanging a request forever, which matters because the Slack side is waiting on it.

A non-OK status becomes an error naming the code, which is how a captcha or a block shows up as something you can read. Then the page text goes to the parser, along with the route, the date and the link, since the page itself does not repeat them.

Terminal use. import.meta.main is true only when this file is the one you ran, so importing it from the tools does nothing. It reads the arguments, searches and prints the five cheapest, which is the fastest way to check whether Google changed the page without starting the whole bot.
